title: New to Al trading & setting a goal: Starting small to fund a Grand Seiko watch (Looking for tips/roadmap)
author: mccamatt92
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m completely new to AI trading and looking to start a practical challenge for myself. My realistic, short-to-medium-term goal isn't to hit a massive fortune, but to make enough extra profit to fund a Grand Seiko watch.

Since I want to keep risk low while I learn, I’d love some tips on how to approach this the right way. My plan is to start smallish and build up gradually.

A few specific questions I have for the community:

 \* What are the best tools, screeners, or platforms for a beginner to start testing AI-assisted strategies without jump-starting into real risk?

 \* Is it generally better to start using AI strictly for technical screening/research, or for automated trade execution via APIs?

 \* What are the biggest hidden traps or red flags I should look out for early on?

Any advice, recommended reading, or roadmap suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
use AI for research and screening first, not execution. the early trap is a backtest that looks great because it quietly used information it couldn't have had at the time, or filled at prices nobody would give you. paper trade it a few weeks before real money goes in.

that testing stage is what Quantradin covers, which I built: write the rule in plain English, it gets checked on past prices with no peeking ahead, then runs on fake money.
quantradin.com

stocks or options for the watch fund?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: then start with plain stocks. options put expiry and a spread on top of every early mistake, and it's easier to learn whether the rule works without them.

comments.author: Electrical_Waltz_888
comments.body:
I’d separate the watch goal from the trading experiment. It’s a good savings target, but needing trading to pay for something within a deadline can create pressure to take more risk. Starting with a small amount limits the dollars exposed; it doesn’t make a strategy low risk.

For learning, I’d start with AI-assisted research and paper trading before connecting anything to a broker API:

1. Choose one market and learn its trading hours, order types and costs.
2. Write one simple strategy with measurable entry, exit and position-size rules.
3. Use AI to challenge those rules and expose missing decisions.
4. Test with fees and realistic execution assumptions, then paper trade a fixed version on fresh data.
5. Track whether the system follows the rules separately from whether it makes money.

A useful starting prompt is: “Here is my trading idea: \[idea\]. Identify vague terms, missing risk decisions and assumptions. Ask me questions before suggesting rules. Do not claim the strategy is profitable.”

The traps I’d watch for are guaranteed-return claims, attractive backtests without costs, repeatedly changing rules until the historical results look good, and giving a bot live trading access before understanding its failure handling.

Disclosure: I’m the author of The Complete Guide to AI Powered Trading, published under Bourhan Chmeisse. It covers this learning-to-specification process and includes 50 reusable prompts. It isn’t a profitable strategy or a promise of income.

[https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HNM97TQ9](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HNM97TQ9)

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Using AI for research and screening first is the safer place to start, and automated trading can wait until you've seen how a strategy behaves with fake money. The biggest traps I'd watch for are fees and slippage eating small gains, systems that look great on past data but don't hold up, paid signal groups, and leverage. A price goal like a watch can also push people into bigger risks, so I'd size every trade by what you can afford to lose, not by the target. Cymetica's Bring Your Own Agent runs agents in paper mode on a practice balance, which is a low risk way to learn.
